short_en: No. Intelligence is about how well you think, not about what you conclude. Some of the sharpest minds in history believed in God, and some didn't. What makes faith smart or lazy is whether you use your mind on it.
short_ar: لا. الذكاء يتعلّق بطريقة تفكيرك، لا بالنتيجة التي تصل إليها. بعض ألمع العقول في التاريخ آمنت بالله، وبعضها لم يؤمن. ما يجعل الإيمان ذكيّاً أو كسولاً هو سؤال واحد: هل تُشغّل عقلك فيه أم لا؟
share_en: Faith doesn't ask you to switch off your brain. It asks you to use all of it.
share_ar: الإيمان لا يطلب منك أن تُطفئ عقلك، بل أن تستعمله كلّه.
anim: A bird with one wing labelled "FAITH" spins in circles; a second wing labelled "REASON" appears, and the bird rises toward a light labelled "TRUTH".

en.story:
Francis Collins studied quantum mechanics at Yale, then medicine, and called himself "a rather obnoxious atheist." But as a young doctor he watched very sick patients lean on their faith, and one heart patient asked him: what do you believe? He realised he had rejected faith without ever examining it. A Methodist minister gave him C.S. Lewis's Mere Christianity. At 27 he became a Christian. He went on to lead the Human Genome Project from 1993, and later directed the US National Institutes of Health (2009–2021). (PBS, Salon, Wikipedia)

Honest note: one brilliant believer doesn't prove God exists. It only shows that faith and top-level science can live in the same mind. (Collins also accepts evolution and rejects "intelligent design", so believing scientists don't all agree.)
en.deeper: The Church doesn't ask you to switch off your brain. It asks you to use all of it. St John Paul II opens Fides et Ratio (1998) by calling faith and reason "two wings on which the human spirit rises" toward truth. The Catechism says faith "seeks understanding" (CCC 158) and that real science can never truly conflict with faith, because both come from the same God (CCC 159). Faith itself is trust based on good reasons, not a blindfold (SoA God L1, p. 9). The course adds a twist: the really unthinking position is scientism, the claim that only science gives real knowledge. No experiment can prove that claim, so it refutes itself (SoA God L2, pp. 12–13). A believer who never asks questions is lazy. So is an atheist who never examines his doubts.
en.proof:
• Pew Research Center (2009): 51% of US scientists in the AAAS believe in God (33%) or in a universal spirit or higher power (18%); 41% believe in neither. That is fewer than the general public (95%), but far from "no smart people believe". (Pew)
  • Honest note: a 2013 review of 63 studies found a small average negative link between intelligence test scores and religious belief (mean r ≈ −0.24). It is an average over groups, not a verdict on any person, and it does not prove that one causes the other. Commentators stress the ranges overlap: many highly intelligent people are believers. (PubMed, The Conversation)
